front.title: Head-tilt/chin-lift
front.summary: The default manual airway maneuver.

back.body: In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the most likely obstruction. This maneuver moves the jaw, and the tongue with it, off the back of the throat. It is the first choice when nothing about the mechanism raises a spinal concern.
back.why_it_matters: Its one contraindication is the entire reason the other maneuver exists.

front.title: Head-tilt/chin-lift vs. jaw-thrust
front.summary: Which maneuver, and why.

back.body: Both open the airway. Head-tilt/chin-lift is the default when nothing about the mechanism suggests a spinal injury. Jaw-thrust is for when it does — it gets the jaw forward without the head movement the default requires.
back.why_it_matters: Pick the maneuver that matches how the patient got hurt.

front.title: Oxygen cylinders at a glance
front.summary: Sizes, pressures, and the duration formula.

back.body: Full ~2,000 psi · Swap at 200 psi · D ~350 L (0.16) · E ~625 L (0.28) · M ~3,000 L (1.56) · Duration (min) = (psi − 200) × constant ÷ L/min
back.why_it_matters: The duration calculation and the 200 psi rule are guaranteed exam material and real-world safety.

front.title: Oxygen safety
front.summary: Oxygen is not flammable, but it makes everything else burn.

back.body: No oil, grease, or petroleum near fittings · Secure the cylinder · Away from heat and flame · Open the valve slowly, stand to the side · Check the hydrostatic test date
back.why_it_matters: A sheared valve turns a cylinder into a projectile; a greased fitting can ignite.

front.title: Nasal cannula vs. non-rebreather
front.summary: The two devices you will use on almost every call.

back.body: Cannula: 1 to 6 L/min · 24 to 44% · breathing well, mildly low sat · not for mouth breathers or distress. NRB: 10 to 15 L/min · up to ~90% · breathing adequately, needs high O2 · not for inadequate breathing (use BVM).
back.why_it_matters: Device selection is the single most-tested airway decision at the EMT level.

front.title: Applying a non-rebreather
front.summary: Six steps; four are critical.

back.body: 1. Confirm adequate breathing (critical) · 2. Set 10 to 15 L/min (critical) · 3. Fill the reservoir before applying (critical) · 4. Seal mask, tighten strap · 5. Bag must not collapse more than one-third; raise flow if it does (critical) · 6. Reassess SpO2 and work of breathing
back.why_it_matters: Skipping the reservoir fill or missing inadequate breathing are the two classic errors.

front.title: Partial rebreather vs. Venturi
front.summary: Two masks you need to recognize but rarely use.

back.body: Partial rebreather: no one-way valve, some rebreathing, ~40 to 60%, 6 to 10 L/min, rare in EMS. Venturi: color-coded adapters, precise ~24 to 50%, flow printed on adapter, for controlled FiO2 (some COPD).
back.why_it_matters: The exam asks which device gives a precise concentration and what makes a partial rebreather different.

front.title: When the pulse ox lies
front.summary: Treat the patient, not the number.

back.body: Falsely high: carbon monoxide poisoning. Unreliable: poor perfusion, shock, cold, hypothermia, nail polish or artificial nails, bright light, motion. Normal SpO2 does not rule out inadequate ventilation.
back.why_it_matters: A 99% reading on a fire victim is a trap question and a real-world killer.

front.title: SpO2 ranges
front.summary: What normal looks like and where concern starts.

back.body: Normal: 95 to 100% · Concern in the acutely ill: below 94% · CO poisoning: reads falsely high, never trust
back.why_it_matters: The 94% line is where the oxygen decision starts.

front.title: Oxygen targets
front.summary: Oxygen is a drug. Dose it.

back.body: Most patients: titrate to 94 to 99% · CO2-retaining COPD: ~88 to 92% per protocol, never withhold in distress · High-flow without hesitation: hypoxia, shock, respiratory distress, inadequate breathing, CO poisoning
back.why_it_matters: Routine 15 L/min for everyone is gone; the exam tests whether you know why and who still gets it.

front.title: Nasal cannula
front.summary: Low-flow oxygen for the patient who is breathing well

back.body: Two prongs just inside the nostrils · 1 to 6 L/min · roughly 24 to 44% O2 · For adequate breathing with a mildly low sat · Above 6 L/min: switch device, don't raise flow · Useless for mouth breathers or a blocked nose
back.why_it_matters: The most common device you'll use, and the one most often used wrong by cranking the flow.

front.title: Non-rebreather mask
front.summary: High-concentration oxygen for the patient who is still breathing adequately

back.body: 10 to 15 L/min · Up to ~90% O2 · Fill the reservoir before applying · One-way valves keep exhaled air out · Bag must not collapse more than one-third · Inadequate breathing means BVM, not NRB
back.why_it_matters: The device-selection question between NRB and BVM is on every EMT exam.

front.title: Oxygen is a drug
front.summary: Titrate it like one

back.body: Target 94 to 99% for most patients · Below target: give and adjust · In range and comfortable: no oxygen needed · Routine high-flow for non-hypoxic cardiac and stroke patients is no longer recommended · Hypoxia, shock, distress, inadequate breathing, CO: high-flow now
back.why_it_matters: Reflex 15 L/min for everyone is old practice, and the exam tests whether you know why.

front.title: Upper vs. lower airway
front.summary: The dividing line is the larynx.

back.body: Upper: nose, mouth, pharynx (naso, oro, laryngo), epiglottis, larynx with vocal cords. Lower: trachea, carina, right and left bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli. Gas exchange only in alveoli. Cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring.
back.why_it_matters: Structure names show up as distractors for each other; know which side of the line each sits on.

front.title: The tongue is the obstruction
front.summary: In the unresponsive supine patient, assume the tongue first.

back.body: Loss of muscle tone → tongue falls back against the posterior pharynx → snoring, partial or complete obstruction. Fix: head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust, then an airway adjunct to hold it.
back.why_it_matters: The most common obstruction has the simplest fix, and it is the first airway skill you learn.

front.title: Adult vs. pediatric airway
front.summary: Smaller, softer, more crowded, less reserve.

back.body: Child: large tongue, large occiput (pad under shoulders), narrow airway, narrowest at cricoid, high anterior larynx, floppy U-shaped epiglottis, soft trachea (no hyperextension), fast desaturation. Head tilt: slight for children, neutral for infants.
back.why_it_matters: Every difference is tested, and every difference changes how you position the head.

front.title: Pad the shoulders
front.summary: Why an infant's airway folds when they lie flat.

back.body: The large occiput tips the chin toward the chest and flexes the neck. A folded towel under the shoulders levels the head so the ear canal lines up with the front of the shoulder. Neutral position, no tilt.
back.why_it_matters: The classic pediatric airway question, and a real fix you will use on every unresponsive infant.

front.title: Ventilation, respiration, oxygenation
front.summary: Three different things that fail separately.

back.body: Ventilation: moving air (chest rise). Respiration: gas exchange at the alveoli and at the cells. Oxygenation: oxygen onto hemoglobin and out to tissues. CO poisoning = ventilating, not oxygenating. Slow shallow breathing = not ventilating, CO2 builds up.
back.why_it_matters: The exam asks which one is broken, and chest rise alone never answers that.

front.title: Breathing volumes
front.summary: Tidal volume, dead space, minute volume.

back.body: Tidal volume ~500 mL (adult) · Dead space ~150 mL · Minute volume = TV × rate, normal ~6 to 8 L/min · Alveolar ventilation = (TV − 150) × rate · Normal drive to breathe = rising CO2
back.why_it_matters: Explains why shallow breathing is worse than the rate suggests.

front.title: Normal respiratory rates
front.summary: By age. Memorize all three.

back.body: Adult 12 to 20 · Child (1 to 12 yr) 15 to 30 · Infant (under 1 yr) 25 to 50 · Count 30 seconds × 2 without telling the patient · Normal = regular, even chest rise, quiet, effortless, full sentences
back.why_it_matters: A rate of 28 is normal in a toddler and abnormal in an adult; the exam will ask both.

front.title: Adequate vs. inadequate breathing
front.summary: The decision the whole airway module builds toward.

back.body: Adequate: normal rate for age, regular, even chest rise, quiet, easy, full sentences → oxygen if hypoxic. Inadequate: rate too fast or slow, shallow, irregular, accessory muscles, retractions, flaring, tripod, 2 to 3 word dyspnea → ventilate with BVM. Late: cyanosis, altered mental status, agonal gasps (= not breathing).
back.why_it_matters: Oxygen versus ventilation is the single most important airway decision at the EMT level.

front.title: Signs of effort
front.summary: What working hard to breathe looks like.

back.body: Accessory muscle use (neck, shoulders) · Retractions (skin pulling in between or under ribs) · Nasal flaring · Tripod position · Pursed-lip breathing · Two or three words per breath · Cannot lie flat
back.why_it_matters: Effort is where you catch inadequate breathing before the late signs appear.
